title: Targeting Indicators
author: Adam Boxer
summary: In the sixth entry of his Most Common Actions series, Adam Boxer extends his sampling-statistics framing of classroom questioning into a specific technique: targeting indicator students. He argues that any single question directed at one student is effectively a poll with a sample size of one, and that who gets asked (sample skew) determines how much that answer tells you about the rest of the class - asking the strongest student tells you almost nothing useful, since they were likely to get it right regardless. His proposed fix is to identify the roughly one-third of the class who find the material moderately challenging and preferentially target them when checking for understanding, since a correct answer from an indicator student is a meaningfully stronger signal that the wider class has grasped the content. He anticipates the natural worry this will surface - indicator students getting more visible wrong answers - and reframes it as information being revealed rather than caused: those students weren't secretly understanding everything before, the teacher simply hadn't noticed the gap. Boxer bounds his own claim carefully, describing the technique as just a probabilities game based on a sample size of one, and positions mini-whiteboards, which sample the whole class simultaneously, as the more reliable check-for-understanding tool for a future post in the series.
points: Boxer applies a sampling-statistics lens to classroom questioning, arguing that who you ask (sample skew) and how many you ask (sample size) both determine how valid your inference about whole-class understanding actually is.

His indicator students concept - targeting the rough third of the class who find content moderately tougher - is designed to make a single student's correct answer a genuinely useful proxy for the class, unlike asking the strongest or most eager student.

He anticipates the discomfort of watching indicator students get things wrong more often, reframing it as revealed rather than caused: those students didn't understand before either, the teacher just didn't know it yet.

Boxer is careful to bound the technique's certainty, explicitly calling it just a probabilities game with a sample size of one, and pairs it with mini-whiteboards as the more reliable tool for actually large-sample checks.
quotes: One issue was around a 'skewed sample': these students are extremely likely to know the answer, which means we learn little about class understanding based on them.

Any time you ask a student a question you make an assumption about what others in the room do or don’t know. That assumption is more or less valid depending on which student you ask (sample skew) and how many of them you ask (sample size)

Try and identify the rough third of your class who find things a bit tougher, and consider them your indicators. Then, if you ask them a question and they show strong understanding, you can make a better assumption about class understanding
It’s really important that you note that, because it’s not like up until you started targeting them they understood everything perfectly. They didn’t understand it before: you just didn’t realise.

Make sure to never ask a student a question if they don’t have a better than reasonable chance of getting it right or at least partially right. Doing otherwise will just induce stress and isn’t very nice.

Targeting an indicator increases the chances that we might make better assumptions, but it’s still just a probabilities game. We still have only one student in our sample and make an assumption based on that
